blocks.text: Ask a simple question about Jio in 2018: who is the CEO? Reporters at The Ken found that almost nobody could answer it. The company had more than 100,000 employees and over 160 million subscribers, yet it had ==no CEO and no COO==. The biggest calls sat with Mukesh Ambani, his old friend Manoj Modi and his children Isha and Akash, and groups of presidents and vice-presidents carried them out.
But the buck stops with Mukesh Ambani and Manoj Modi.
blocks.who: A former Jio employee, speaking anonymously to The Ken, 2018

blocks.text: Reliance told The Ken this was a choice, because it wanted Jio to behave like a startup. Compare that with Vodafone at the time, where the big decisions came from London and local chiefs executed them. Or with the Aditya Birla Group, where a named CEO ran the telecom arm. Jio does have a managing director today, Akash Ambani, but the instinct behind that old structure explains how his father works: a very small circle decides, and a very large machine executes.
Org charts are optional. Knowing who decides is not.
The friend with no title

The most important person in that circle met him in college. Manoj Modi studied chemical engineering with Ambani at the University Department of Chemical Technology in Mumbai in the 1970s. When Modi once asked Dhirubhai Ambani for permission to go abroad for a finance master's degree, the patriarch refused. “It’s waste of time, do some work,” he told him.

In 2013 The Economic Times reported that Modi's visiting card carried ==no designation== and that he was not on the board. It also said that if Reliance had a CEO, he would be the man. He was a director at Reliance Retail and Jio by 2020, and Bloomberg reported that a meeting with him often signalled final approval on a deal. In a rare public talk, he played it all down.
In fact, people internally know that I don’t even have a vision.
blocks.who: Manoj Modi, at a Kalaari Capital conference, reported by Bloomberg, 2020

blocks.text: Do not believe the modesty. Air Deccan founder G. R. Gopinath, who sold a stake in his cargo airline to Reliance in 2010, called Modi “ruthlessly efficient”. Venture capitalist Vani Kola, who persuaded Modi to make that rare appearance, said the pair drive “relentless execution to the last level of detail”. __Ambani picks the mountain, and Modi makes sure every rope is tied.__

For example: when Jio was racing to launch and build its fibre network, one person in the talks told Bloomberg that select vendors were called to headquarters and tempted with the sheer size of the project. What the vendors did not know was that several Reliance teams were negotiating at the same moment in separate rooms, with Modi guiding all of them.
Met at college. Decades later, still closing his biggest deals.
How a decision gets made

In 2011, long before anyone had heard the word Jio, The Economic Times got a two-hour look at the process. Ambani and Modi were moderating “fierce debates” among a team of just eight or nine people. They were trying to work out the shape of a digital business. The opening question was almost childish: do you know how many bank accounts you have, and would you not like one screen that shows them all?
Business opportunity (in digital services) lies in what you cannot do. What you can do, there’s no opportunity there.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani, Economic Times, 2011

blocks.text: People who have sat across from him describe a listener. Lawyer Zia Mody says “he listens closely to the views of others, processes them and then takes his decision, and is fully accountable to his team for that.” KKR India's former chairman Sanjay Nayar remembers that “he’s all yours in a meeting.” These are business associates speaking warmly about an important client or partner, so read them that way.

His attention is not spread evenly. Industrialist Harsh Goenka, a friend for almost four decades, says the kick for Ambani is a new venture, where he “often spends about 80 percent of his time.” During the Jio build, Modi ran things day to day while progress reports and briefings reached Ambani's desk at least once a week, according to a person quoted by The Economic Times. Jio was also built to be centralised, with most decisions taken in Mumbai and left to the regional circles only to execute.
Why he banned the hero

His management idea was born in the early 1980s, when he came home to build the polyester plant. The rule from his father was blunt: build it from scratch, without taking anyone from Reliance. Within three months he noticed something odd. The whole industry ran on “heroes”, experts who wrote the temperatures and pressures in private notebooks and carried them home.
we don’t want people carrying their wisdom in notebooks as if it is some kind of secretive operation.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani, MoneyLIFE interview, 2007

blocks.text: So he wrote everything into standard operating procedures that the whole plant could see. It looked like paperwork. Then came the test. Rasikbhai, one of the three people running the business, died on 30 August 1985, and Dhirubhai had a stroke the following February. For a while, Mukesh Ambani, then in his twenties, was alone at the top.
There was no sense of panic. The whole picture was in my head.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani on the 1985–86 crisis, MoneyLIFE, 2007

blocks.text: Write it down. If only one person knows it, you have a hero problem.

The same thinking shaped how he bought knowledge. Competitors were paying half a million to a million dollars for licences, while Reliance, short of capital, agreed to pay DuPont ==$5 million== to work with the best. Then it did the clever part. It brought in a few DuPont experts and put 25-year-olds beside them to learn how to run the chemical processes.
Young people, big jobs

His father's rule was “Always keep the average age of Reliance at 30”. In 1998, Ambani said nearly Rs 500 billion of assets had been built by a team with an average age under 35. The habit has survived. In 2023–24, ==53.9%== of Reliance Group employees were under 30, and so were 81.8% of new hires.

Young does not mean unguided. For the Jio build, The Economic Times reported a plan to hire two sets of leaders for some senior roles: an Indian with domain knowledge and an expat who could advise on global practice. Reliance also says it picks high performers aged 30 to 35 and trains them as future leaders.

For example: when Reliance signed its $7.2 billion deal with BP in London, people noticed Akash Ambani in the room and assumed the heir was being groomed. His father pointed out that three other Reliance trainees were there too. “I asked them to come along and see how it feels,” he said.

And what does he look for? Not degrees first. In 2025 he told McKinsey that the people process focuses on character, because it matters that people can trust each other. His theory of motivation is just as simple: “if you can win a person’s heart, their mind will work for you.”
Character is even more important than competence because competence can be built.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani, McKinsey interview, 2025

blocks.text: The other side of the machine

A company this size also churns people, and the numbers are public. In FY24 the Reliance headcount fell by ==42,052==, and retail alone accounted for 38,029 of that. Hiring was cut by more than a third. Reliance noted that retail has high turnover, especially in stores, and one staffing expert said some roles may simply have moved to third-party payrolls, so this was not 42,000 sackings.

items.label: Reliance Group workforce, FY24, down from 3,89,414
People who left on their own in that one year

blocks.text: One retail consultant told The Economic Times that managements were now “highly objective, even ruthless” about shutting stores that did not pay. Harsh Goenka has noted that in the early retail years many professionals came and left. Modi could be rough too: The Economic Times described him dealing with vendors “often in an aggressive language” and growling at anyone who crossed the boss.

Here we must be honest about a gap. Former Reliance employees rarely speak on the record, and we did not find a named one describing how Ambani hires or fires people in person. Reliance does not advertise its structure either, as Kola pointed out. So treat this picture as what it is: built from his own words, business associates, press reports and company numbers.
His hours, his habits

Nobody has published a verified diary, and the reports do not agree. A 2009 Times of India profile had him reaching the office at noon and working until midnight, and Open magazine said in 2020 that he works late and starts before noon. Nita Ambani said in 2013 that he gets home very late, but they make sure to eat dinner together. Newer lifestyle pieces describe a 5:30 am yoga start, which we could not trace to a first-hand source, though she has said he does yoga and meditation regularly.

Other details from that 2009 profile: he likes long walks with a colleague as brainstorming sessions, reads management books and tries out what they say, and colleagues claim they have never known him to shout. In 2011 he was studying memos by the management thinker C. K. Prahalad while working out how to “institutionalise” Reliance. A former executive told Open that Walter Isaacson is his favourite writer.
Notice the pattern: read widely, walk, argue, then decide.

chapters.title: Eight Things He Won't Compromise On

blocks.text: Mukesh Ambani is not a man of many interviews, which makes the few he has given unusually useful. Read them side by side, from 1998 to 2025, and the same ideas keep returning. Here are eight of them, each with a story.
1. Chase a billion people, not a billion dollars
My father used to say that if you want to start a business to be a billionaire, you are an idiot; you will never get there.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani, quoting Dhirubhai Ambani, McKinsey interview, 2025

blocks.text: The other half of that line is the point. If you want to impact a billion people, his father said, you have a good chance of success, and you can make “a reasonable amount of money” as a by-product. Ambani says Reliance starts every new business with one question: what is the most critical need for India's development, and how can it be met at scale over a long arc of time? You can find that a bit grand, coming from one of the world's richest men. But it did tell him which businesses to enter.
Read this twice. Impact first. The money is the side effect.
2. First ask: can we survive the worst day?

People see Ambani as a gambler. His own rule is about survival. “The principle is whether you can survive in the worst-comes-to-the-worst situation,” he told McKinsey. You begin by imagining the worst that could happen, and then you make sure you can live through it.

In 2011 he explained this using an animal. He told The Economic Times that he had spent hours watching leopards in forests, and that Reliance should learn from them. At the time he was sitting on a cash pile of Rs 42,000 crore, and he said “we’ll never do it for ego’s sake.”
It doesn’t take any risk. Whenever it sees it can make a kill, it rapidly makes the kill.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani on the leopard, Economic Times, 2011

blocks.text: Five years later he made the biggest kill attempt of his life. Analysts doubted India was ready for advanced digital networks, so he told the board what the worst case looked like: a poor return on the company's own money, and a digitised India anyway. __He did not bet that nothing could go wrong. He decided in advance that he could live with what went wrong.__
In the worst case, we will not earn much return. That’s okay because it’s our own money.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani, recalling what he told the Reliance board about Jio, McKinsey, 2025

blocks.text: 3. Ordinary people plus a clear framework

He is suspicious of geniuses. In the 1980s his reference points were American chemical companies, especially DuPont, with a huge US bias and a handful of outstanding managers from India's public sector. One of them, K. K. Malhotra, stayed for 15 years from 1985. “He was my guru,” Ambani says, and he came from the public sector, not from Silicon Valley.
I always believe that so-called ordinary people can achieve extraordinary results as long they are given a sensible framework.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani, MoneyLIFE, 2007

blocks.text: Eighteen years later he made the same point to McKinsey. He said that “individually, all of us have great potential, but we are limited by our habits,” and that organisations are limited by their systems and structures. He says the books already contain the right answers. The real work is closing the gap between what is written, what the shop floor does and what the marketplace wants. That, he says, is execution.
4. Say no to the good thing

Here is a detail few people know. In the 1990s, Reliance signed a joint venture with ==Microsoft==. Ambani had lived in Silicon Valley, knew software was a giant opportunity, and even spoke about it in a 1995 speech. Then he walked away from the Microsoft deal.
we have too much soap on our body and we need to take a bath in the chemicals business.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani on why he passed on IT, MoneyLIFE, 2007

blocks.text: Asked whether that meant missing the bus, he did not flinch. “To my mind, I was right,” he said. You may disagree: India's IT services boom happened without Reliance. But the logic is clear. He would not start a second bath while still covered in soap from the first.

The opposite move came when something threatened the core. Around 1996–97, Dow announced it would make plastics using E. coli. Reliance was already big in plastics and feared being ruined, so it quickly put four or five people on the problem. That defensive scramble is how it entered biotech.

Then, in the late 1990s, with cash flowing, his father told him, “now it is your call, what you would like to do.” He chose to use the money for businesses of the future, and that is how Infocomm was born.
Focus is not 'no forever'. It is 'not until the soap is off'.
5. Let the young overrule you

Ambani says that when he was about 14, his father told him he was not under training: “You are my partner and this is your responsibility.” He says he has done the same with his children and with the 30-year-olds at Reliance. The story that proves it is now famous. Isha came home from Yale and said, “Dad, the internet in our house sucks.” His first reaction, as he told it in 2016, was to insist it was the best internet available.

Then Akash told him, “Dad, you won’t get it.” In the old telecom world, Akash explained, you earn money only when one person phones another and the other picks up. In his world, he just talks to a server, and there is never a no-reply. A father worth billions took notes. That idea later became a $25 billion bet.
My children boss over me. It’s a new life. It’s good for me.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani, 2016

blocks.text: In his fifties, he was learning telecom from his kids. What's your excuse?
6. Own the technology

When he was young, Indian companies licensed technology from abroad and could “lose your shirt” if a plan failed. So he pushed his leaders to become owners of technology. For 5G, Reliance built most of the system itself and used Ericsson and Nokia for about 20%. His reason is a little wicked.
I also wanted to make sure that our people were not too full of themselves.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani on keeping Ericsson and Nokia in the 5G build, McKinsey, 2025

blocks.text: He told his engineers, “You have to be better than these guys.” Keeping a world-class rival inside your own project is a test as well as a safety net. Every day, your team can see the standard.
7. The Rs 10 rule

This may be the most copyable idea in this book. He sets an impossible cost target before he has any idea how to reach it. Whatever America builds in dollars, he wants India to build as if a dollar were worth only Rs 10. “When we start off, this looks impossible,” he said. “Then we think through it, value-engineer it and come close to it.”
I always say whatever the US implements in dollars we should be able to do it at exchange rate of Rs 10, then we would be globally competitive.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani, MoneyLIFE, 2007

blocks.text: For example: he also looks for price gaps that nobody is exploiting. “From Bill Gates to my driver, everybody eats potatoes,” he said in 2007. Farmers in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar got about Rs 4–5 a kilo, while the same potato was Rs 25–30 wholesale in the Middle East, Rs 90 at Sam's Club in the US and Rs 110 in Europe. That is a gap of 1:20, and to him it was the same kind of arbitrage that built India's software exports.
8. Build something that outlasts you

His mind keeps returning to a sentence from his father. “Reliance is a process. It’s an institution that should last.” He calls the promise that it will outlive him his commitment to his father, and he says he wants Reliance serving India after it turns 100. He also says business strategy should change every three, four or five years, while the goal stays fixed.

That is why he talks about culture as a risk tool. About 30 or 40 years ago, he says, he made himself a personal principle: he must be able to look any employee in the eye. Reliance tells its top 100 leaders the same thing, that “we should be able to look at each other and say we are not embarrassed.” He calls this culture “our best insurance against any kind of risk.” As later chapters show, regulators and critics have not always been so sure, which is exactly why the test is worth remembering.
You come without anything into this world, and you leave without taking anything with you.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani, McKinsey interview, 2025

chapters.kicker: Family, food and a very tall house
chapters.title: The Man Behind the Tower

blocks.text: Start with Sundays. Ambani says that for his father, Reliance was his whole life, yet “Sunday was for his wife and kids” no matter how much pressure there was, and it was not for homework. They walked through forests and bathed in streams. He says he tries to do the same with his own family, and he became a big nature lover himself.

His father never came to his school, not even once, and left him to choose his own subjects. He tried to bring up his own children the same way and admitted he could not always manage it. When Isha and Akash were in class three, he said, the parents behaved as though it was their own exam. He joked that he could beat any parent his age in the ICSE syllabus, until his daughter told him she had to study it herself.
A billionaire memorising the ICSE syllabus. His daughter told him to stop.
Nita

Nita Ambani grew up, as she has described it, a middle-class girl who travelled by bus and train in Mumbai. Hindustan Times reported that Dhirubhai noticed her at a dance performance. She became the public face of the family's giving, heading Reliance Foundation, and served on the Reliance board until she stepped down in 2023 to focus on it. In a 2018 speech, he publicly called her his life-partner and thanked her for her “steadfast support”.

Her description of him is domestic. “He reaches home very late in the evening but we make it a point to have dinner together,” she said in 2013. They holidayed mostly in the jungles of India and Africa, she said. The paper also reported that the children got just Rs 5 each in pocket money when small and were not unfamiliar with public transport. Asked what she would change about him, she chose “his love for food!”
Idli, films and no birthday parties

Food is his one admitted weakness. He told Upper Crust magazine that the family eats home-cooked vegetarian food, and that he also ate eggs. “Idli-sambar drives me wild!” he said, adding that he could eat it anywhere, even at small airport canteens. Nita said in 2024 that he remains on a strict vegetarian diet of mainly home food.

His other escape is the screen. The Times of India reported in 2009 that he loved Hindi films, did not miss a single one, and that friends swore by his verdict on whether a film would be a hit. James Crabtree wrote of late-night Bollywood films in Antilia's home cinema, and a former executive told Open that his favourite film is The Godfather. The same 2009 profile says he had never celebrated a birthday except his 50th, with employees at the Jamnagar plant.
The brother

The most painful chapter of his personal life was public from the start. After Dhirubhai died in 2002 without a will, the brothers fell out. Both lived in the same family tower, Sea Wind, on separate floors, and during the feud they ==co-ordinated their entry and exit== to avoid meeting in the lift. Their mother Kokilaben lived in the same building. The business story of that fight is in the next chapters. Here, what matters is how it ended, and who ended it.
With the blessings of Srinathji, I have today amicably resolved the issues between my two sons, Mukesh and Anil
blocks.who: Kokilaben Ambani, statement, June 2005

blocks.text: Fourteen years later came a twist no scriptwriter would dare. In February 2019, the Supreme Court gave Anil Ambani four weeks to pay Swedish company Ericsson, or spend three months in jail. On 18 March, one day before the deadline, the money arrived. Anil issued a statement thanking his brother and sister-in-law. People familiar with the matter told ET Telecom that Mukesh contributed around ==Rs 480 crore==, as an outright payment and not a loan, though Reuters said the nature of the backing was unclear.
I and my family are grateful we have moved beyond the past, and are deeply touched with this gesture
blocks.who: Anil Ambani, statement, 18 March 2019

blocks.text: Rivals for 15 years. He still paid before the jail door closed.
A son's health, and a father's tears

The family itself has spoken publicly about their youngest son's health, so we repeat only that. Nita Ambani said in 2013 that Anant was fighting obesity, and in a 2025 interview she linked his struggle to asthma. At his pre-wedding celebration in Jamnagar in March 2024, Anant spoke about it himself in front of the guests, and his father wept.
my life has not always been entirely a bed of roses. I have also experienced the pain of thorns.
blocks.who: Anant Ambani, Jamnagar, March 2024

blocks.text: It was a rare public show of emotion from a very private man. It would not be the last. You will see him cry again in the final chapter of this book.
The car outside the house

On 25 February 2021, a Scorpio SUV with 20 sticks of gelatin and a threatening letter was found near Antilia. The head of security at the residence later told investigators that Nita Ambani's planned trip to Jamnagar was rescheduled and then cancelled on his and the police's advice. The Ambani family did not suspect any particular person, he said. Then the case took a dark turn. The car's owner, Mansukh Hiran, was found dead on 5 March, and the first lead investigator, police officer Sachin Waze, was arrested.

In August 2026 a special NIA court framed charges against ten people, including Waze, on charges including murder and terror offences. They have pleaded not guilty, and the trial is still ahead, so nothing here is a finding of guilt. The NIA alleges the motive was to terrorise wealthy people and extort money. These remain allegations.
How he spends money

The first answer is surprising. From 2008–09 to 2019–20 he capped his own pay at Rs 15 crore, which the company described as a personal example of moderation. Since the Covid year he has taken ==nothing==: no salary, perks or stock options for six straight years to FY26. His money comes from owning the company, and his promoter group entities collected close to Rs 4,000 crore in dividends. A salary of zero is cheap when your family group holds half the firm, but plenty of owners still take the cheque.

items.label: Self-imposed annual pay cap, FY09 to FY20
Salary every year from FY21 to FY26
FY26 dividend income through promoter entities

blocks.text: The second answer is impossible to miss. Antilia, finished around 2010, has 27 floors, and press reports put its value at $1 billion or more, though Bloomberg's wealth index lists his Mumbai residential property at just ==$410 million==. A guest told Crabtree, “The chandeliers have chandeliers.” And in 2009 he reportedly owned Bentley and Maybach cars while wearing white shirts and saying “I wear anything that fits me”. Clothes brands do not interest him, by that account. Scale does, and at home he built it.
Giving

The EdelGive Hurun India Philanthropy List ranked Ambani and family ==second in India== for FY25 with Rs 626 crore, up Rs 219 crore. Shiv Nadar and family, far less wealthy, gave Rs 2,708 crore. By our rough maths, Rs 626 crore is about $75 million, or under 0.1% of a fortune of about $80 billion today. Fairness demands one addition: Reliance as a company separately spent Rs 1,309 crore on CSR that year, and Rs 2,248 crore in FY26, the highest of any Indian company, it says.

Some gifts are personal. In June 2025 he gave Rs 151 crore to his old college, the Institute of Chemical Technology in Mumbai, as guru dakshina to his mentor, Professor M. M. Sharma. And in the terrible April of 2021, Reliance said it reconfigured plants at Jamnagar to make medical-grade liquid oxygen, going from nil to over 1,000 tonnes a day, and supplied it free to states. The company's own account says he personally supervised the work.
A refinery became an oxygen plant. Scale can serve in a crisis too.

In 2007, the MoneyLIFE editors opened their interview with a neat summary: Dhirubhai was a larger-than-life patriarch, Anil was the public face of Reliance, and Mukesh was “an enigma”. Very little was known of his beliefs. It was the most expansive interview he had given, and he was already 49 and running Reliance.

Nine years later, in front of a packed Mumbai hall, journalist Shekhar Gupta asked him why he rarely did events like this. His answer, in a wonderfully dry line, was that nobody had asked. Then he gave the real reason.
I generally think that I should only speak by action and not by words
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani, Off The Cuff with Shekhar Gupta, 2016

blocks.text: Most founders post first and build later. He does the reverse.

Those around him share the habit. Reliance does not advertise its structure, and Manoj Modi would appear quietly at the side of the shareholder meeting to brief journalists, then vanish. “Why talk needlessly when you can show your capabilities in the ranbhoomi,” said Vani Kola, using the Hindi word for battlefield. We also found no verified personal social media account for him. Reliance's own pages speak instead.
One big stage a year

So when does he speak? Mainly at one event. His father built that stage, addressing giant crowds of small shareholders at football grounds and cricket pitches. The son made the annual general meeting his main stage. In 2023 he used it to put all three of them on the board, and in 2026 he announced the Jio filing there, calling it “a deeply emotional moment”.

Read the speeches and you see a style. Short sentences. Big round numbers in capital letters. A nation in every paragraph. “Our mission and passion at Reliance is to make India prosperous,” he said in London in 2018, then he told a story no finance director would ever have written.

For example: accepting a Financial Times award in London in March 2018, he did not start with spectrum or capex. He started with his daughter complaining that “the internet in our house sucks”. That one line travelled far. It was still being retold in the international press that September.

__Notice what the story does.__ It turns a $25 billion gamble by the country's richest family into a dad being told off by his kids. A young reader can picture it instantly. It is also, as he told it, slightly different each time: in 2016 he said 2010, and in 2018 he said 2011. Good stories get polished, so always check the dates.
Saying nothing, loudly

Silence has limits, as Antilia showed. When the tower was finished, people asked what he was trying to prove. Then they asked why he had not moved in, and the New York Times reported that he and his spokesman declined to discuss it. Rumours about Vastu faults filled the gap. It was finally Nita who confirmed they had moved in, in a 2012 Vanity Fair interview, after months of what the writer called “nuclear-treaty-level negotiations”, according to James Crabtree.

Then came a very public jab. In May 2011, The Times of London quoted Ratan Tata asking about the house, “It makes me wonder why someone would do that”. Tata Sons quickly said the report was out of context and sensationalised, and that the remarks were about wider inequality, while The Times stood by its story. A local journalist also got hold of Antilia's monthly energy bill, reportedly Rs 7 million, which caused its own outcry.
Silence protects you until someone else starts writing the story.
Close to power

Few things shape his image in India more than his relationship with the government. In September 2016, Jio launched with advertisements showing Prime Minister Narendra Modi's photograph. In December that year, the government told Parliament that the Prime Minister's Office had not given permission. Critics, including Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal, attacked the campaign sharply.

At the 2026 AGM, his very first paragraph congratulated Modi on being the longest-serving elected Prime Minister of India. Opposition leaders have long said Modi is too close to tycoons like Ambani, and Reuters reported posters welcoming the Prime Minister lining the road to the venue of Anant's 2024 wedding. Ambani's supporters see an entrepreneur backing his country. His critics see something else. You should know that both views exist, and that neither is a court finding.

Anger can leave the debating hall. During the 2020–21 farmer protests, angry at new farm laws, protesters in Punjab cut power and damaged Jio sites, and ==over 1,500 of 9,000 towers== there were knocked out in December. Farmers believed Reliance would profit from the laws. The company went to the Punjab and Haryana High Court, said it had “absolutely no plans” to enter contract farming, and blamed “vested interests” and business rivals. Airtel and Vodafone Idea called that baseless.
Spectacle

Having stayed out of sight for decades, the family then became impossible to miss. The Guardian said they spent almost $100 million on Isha's 2018 wedding, where Beyoncé sang. For Anant's in 2024, Rihanna performed at a pre-wedding party, Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg were on the guest list, and Reliance's official Facebook page helped publicise the events. An unnamed Reliance executive called it a “powerful symbol of India’s growing stature on the global stage”.

Not everyone agreed. “Legally it may be their money but such ostentatious expenditure is a sin against mother earth and [the] poor,” opposition politician Thomas Isaac wrote. Residents complained about closed roads during monsoon flooding. Nita Ambani's reply was the one any parent might give: “Every parent wants to do the best for their child,” she said, adding that it showcased Indian tradition.
How the world sees him

At home, he is several people at once. To millions of small investors, he is the heir to a family that made them money: Reliance has returned about 900% since 2006, and over 1.3 crore people applied for the Jio IPO. To others, Antilia is a source of what campaigner Meera Sanyal described to Crabtree as “rage”. Crabtree's book made the house a symbol of India's new Gilded Age.

Abroad, he is a statesman of sorts. The Guardian's headline called the family “the Windsors of India”, the FT gave Reliance its Drivers of Change award, and in October 2026 US Secretary of State Marco Rubio toured Jamnagar with him. Reuters and Bloomberg use the same shorthand: Asia's richest, or near it. Far fewer readers know the man who passed up Microsoft. Most know the tower.

items.text: Says in a TV interview there are “ownership issues” with Anil. The feud goes public.
Antilia is finished, and the tower becomes a national argument.
Jio launches. Modi's photo in the ads causes a row.
Tells the “internet sucks” story to London's business elite.
Helps save brother Anil from jail.
Anant's wedding sets off a global debate about inequality.
Sits in the audience and cries as his children list Jio.

blocks.text: It is easy to write this man's story as one long victory. It was not. Some of his biggest bets lost money or dragged through courts for almost twenty years. Some he still defends. Below is the record, with outcomes, because you will learn more from these pages than from any Jio success story.
The family war

Dhirubhai left no will, assuming his sons would run Reliance together. In July 2004 a board resolution known as Item 17 redefined the managing directors' roles, and Anil protested that it let Mukesh cut him down. In November, Mukesh told a TV reporter about “ownership issues” in the “private domain”, which he later said was torn out of context. Anil publicly blamed “chamchas, chelas and cronies”. Mukesh's camp later accused Anil of a “self-serving media campaign”.

Their mother split the empire in June 2005. Look at what it cost him. Reliance Infocomm, his own telecom project, went to Anil, along with a non-compete deal that shut him out of telecom until it was cancelled in May 2010. He then spent years in court over gas prices against his own brother, winning in the Supreme Court on 7 May 2010. __The fight over the past blocked him from the future for five years.__
Very important for co-founders: write it down while you still like each other.

He seems to have learned. In 2020 Mint reported he was setting up a family council, and in 2021 Bloomberg reported he had studied the Waltons and the Kochs for a structure that could prevent another war. Reliance has not formally confirmed these reports.
The retail promises

In January 2007, freshly launched into retail, he told MoneyLIFE that organised retail could bring ==1.5 million jobs== in three years and raise farm incomes by 600–900%. He added a caveat: “We might be wrong in some of them”. Within months, thousands of vegetable sellers vandalised three Reliance Fresh stores in eastern India. In August 2007, Uttar Pradesh ordered Reliance stores in Lucknow and Varanasi closed, after traders attacked them the day they opened.

What went wrong? Scale frightened the small traders and vendors whose livelihoods it touched, and big talk about farm incomes did not reassure them. Goenka has noted many professionals coming and going. The business survived, and Reliance now reports 20,160 stores. But it needed almost two decades, and in FY24 it still cut staff and closed stores that did not pay. Being right in 20 years does not save you from being attacked in the first one.
The gas field that ran dry

In 2006 Reliance told the government its KG-D6 fields would produce ==80 million standard cubic metres of gas a day==, after raising the plan from $2.47 billion to $8.18 billion. Actual output was 35.33 in 2011–12, 20.88 the next year and 9.77 the year after. Reserve estimates were cut from 10.03 to 3.10 trillion cubic feet, and the D1 and D3 fields stopped producing in February 2020, far earlier than planned. Only 22 of 31 planned wells were drilled.

Who is at fault is still being fought over. The government says Reliance failed to follow the approved plan, disallowed $3.02 billion of costs and has now sought more than $30 billion. Reliance and BP blame unexpected geology, and say all spending was approved by a committee that included government officials. The arbitrators finished hearings in November 2025 and we found no reported award yet. A separate 2011 government audit also criticised the oil ministry's oversight.

There is a second, separate gas case. The government says Reliance and partners were unjustly enriched by gas that migrated from ONGC's neighbouring blocks. Arbitrators ruled for Reliance 2:1 in 2018, a High Court judge agreed in 2023, then a two-judge bench overturned it all in February 2025. The ministry raised a ==$2.81 billion== demand, which Reliance calls unsustainable. On 30 October 2026, the Supreme Court appointed former judge Ranjana Desai as mediator. It is unresolved.
A forecast given to government becomes a promise. Promise only what you can drill.
Shopping in Texas at the top

In 2010, Reliance charged into American shale, buying into Atlas's Marcellus acreage for $1.7 billion, Pioneer's Eagle Ford for about $1.3 billion and a Carrizo venture for $392 million. Then oil crashed in late 2014. By 2016 it had put in about ==$8.2 billion== across its ventures. The Carrizo stake bought for $392 million sold for just $126 million in 2017, and Reliance took a Rs 3,261 crore impairment. It left American shale completely in November 2021.

Be fair: one piece worked. The Eagle Ford midstream venture brought in about $1 billion on $254 million put in. And Reliance said its final sale was above the value on its books, after those write-downs. No public number gives a total loss, so we will not invent one. The lesson is simpler. A year before he praised the patient leopard, he had jumped down from the tree in the middle of someone else's excitement.
Nineteen years in the regulator's shadow

In November 2007, Reliance sold about 5% of its subsidiary Reliance Petroleum. Before that, it signed agreements with 12 entities that took short positions in the futures market, with the profits flowing back to Reliance. In the last minutes of the settlement day, large share sales hit the market. In 2017 SEBI called this manipulation, ordered Reliance to give up Rs 447 crore plus 12% interest, and banned it from equity derivatives for a year.

items.text: SEBI orders Rs 447 crore disgorgement and a one-year derivatives ban. Reliance serves the ban.
Tribunal upholds SEBI by 2:1. Its chair dissents, saying fraud was not proved.
SEBI fines Reliance Rs 25 crore and Mukesh Ambani personally Rs 15 crore.
Tribunal quashes the Rs 15 crore fine on him.
Supreme Court dismisses SEBI's appeal against that relief. “You can’t chase a person like this for years,” the bench says.
Supreme Court overturns the fraud finding and the Rs 447 crore order, and orders Rs 250 crore refunded.

blocks.text: So who won? Mostly Reliance. The Supreme Court held that the 12 agreements “were not a device used for fraud and manipulation”, and it said the tribunal made an “egregious error”. But the win was partial. The court agreed Reliance had broken disclosure rules on position limits and left the penalty in place. __Being cleared after 19 years is still 19 years.__
The deal he announced too early

In 2019 he told the world Saudi Aramco would buy 20% of Reliance's oil-to-chemicals business for about $15 billion, a major plank in his debt-cutting plan. It was a non-binding agreement. Two years of talks followed. On 19 November 2021 the companies said they would “re-evaluate”, and Reuters sources said valuation was the sticking point as the world moved away from fossil fuels. The shares fell 4.2%.

He got away with it, because the Jio stake sales to Meta, Google and others made Reliance net-debt free anyway. But the Future Group deal showed the same weakness. Agreed in August 2020 for Rs 24,713 crore, it was attacked by Amazon in court and finally dead in April 2022, when Future's secured creditors voted it down. Big announcements and finished deals are two different things.
When winning hurts others

Jio's free calls and cheap data were great for customers. For rivals, they were a brutal shock. Airtel filed a predatory pricing complaint, which the Competition Commission rejected in June 2017, because Jio held only 6.4% of subscribers and “providing free services cannot by itself raise competition concerns” without dominance. Legal, then.
ET Telecom later reported smaller operators shutting and Idea and Vodafone merging. RCom, the company run by his own brother, was among the casualties. Then he helped keep that brother out of jail.

A young founder should think hard about this. A strategy that needs about $25 billion of someone's cash pile is not one you can copy. And a market with very few survivors has its own price, which is more political attention than most founders would ever want.
Family and governance

Critics also ask how a listed company picks its leaders. Proxy adviser IiAS urged shareholders to vote against Anant Ambani's 2023 board seat, because he was under 30. He won with 92.75% of the votes, against 98.21% for Isha and 98.05% for Akash. In 2025 IiAS and SES opposed his appointment as whole-time director, citing experience and unclear pay. Reliance replied that he had worked in the group since 2015. Promoters hold about half the votes, so ordinary resolutions like these tend to pass.

One more case deserves careful wording. Anant's animal rescue centre, Vantara, faced complaints of smuggling and mistreatment. A Supreme Court-appointed team, led by a former judge, found no legal violation, and on 15 September 2025 the Court accepted that and closed the complaints. Weeks later, a report by the CITES Secretariat did not find imports without permits, but said India's due diligence had gaps and urged a pause on some imports. The Court cleared it, and an international body still had questions.
Winning in court and winning public trust are separate exams.

Mumbai, 28 October 2026. At the National Stock Exchange, the Ambani family gathers on stage. Before walking up to speak, Akash, the 35-year-old managing director of Jio Platforms, touches his parents' feet. All three children speak. Their father, 69, does not give a speech. He sits in the audience, next to Nita, and he is in tears.

Isha reminded the room that Reliance's 1977 IPO raised Rs 2.82 crore. Jio's raised around ==Rs 30,213 crore==, the largest in India's history. The issue filled in 95 minutes and drew Rs 7.5 lakh crore of demand. Shares offered at Rs 1,119 closed the first day at Rs 1,417.50, and Jio became India's second most valuable listed company, behind only its parent.
Today, the bell at the Exchange will ring for me like a temple bell
blocks.who: Anant Ambani, Jio listing ceremony, 28 October 2026

blocks.text: He built it for ten years. Then he let his kids hold the mic.
His job now

He remains Chairman and Managing Director of Reliance Industries. At the August 2023 AGM he committed to five more years, “with greater vigour”, and listed his three duties: groom next-generation leaders, mentor Akash, Isha and Anant so they can lead together, and enrich the culture. India Today read that as stepping down at about 71, around 2028–29. We found no published handover date.

The split is already visible: Akash at Jio, Isha at retail, Anant in new energy and now an executive director. Back at Family Day in December 2021, he had described his duty in words any good teacher would recognise.
We should guide them, enable them, encourage them and empower them... and sit back and applaud as they perform better than us
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani, Reliance Family Day, December 2021

blocks.text: The numbers behind him

items.label: Reliance FY26 revenue ($124.0 billion), a record
FY26 EBITDA, more than double the FY21 figure, as he promised

blocks.text: The bets on the table

The first is artificial intelligence. On 19 February 2026, at the India AI Impact Summit in New Delhi, he pledged ==Rs 10 lakh crore over seven years==, about $110 billion. He made the same argument he made about data ten years ago: compute is scarce and costly, and “India cannot afford to rent intelligence.” Reuters noted the sum is modest beside what American giants plan. The first 120 megawatts at Jamnagar are due by the end of 2026, with Google and Meta as partners.

The second is clean energy, which he calls Reliance's most ambitious generational undertaking. At the 2026 AGM, he reported nearly 1 GW of solar modules made at Jamnagar and a 40 GWh battery plant due this year, to be expanded to 120 GWh. He also described a renewable hub on 5,50,000 acres in Kutch and a $3 billion green ammonia contract with Samsung C&T. He admits it has been harder than any roadmap anticipated.
We ask for your continued trust. And we intend to earn it – quarter by quarter.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani on new energy, 49th AGM, June 2026

blocks.text: The third is the old business. Retail and digital now make nearly half of EBITDA, which means oil, chemicals and everything else still make about half. Forbes blamed margin pressure at retail for part of his wealth decline this year, and Nikkei flagged volatility in the core oil business around the IPO. Reuters says the plan is to turn Reliance into an “everything company”. Rubio's tour of Jamnagar in October, which covered both conventional and new energy, shows the refinery still gets the world's attention.
What he is worth, and why it is a bit strange

Forbes put him at ==$80.3 billion, ranked 25th in the world,== on 1 November 2026. Bloomberg put him at $77.3 billion and 24th, down about $27 billion from a year ago. So just after his greatest triumph, he was getting poorer on paper: on the morning after the listing, Forbes showed him as one of the day's biggest wealth losers. The Forbes India list, published in late September and counting family fortunes, placed Gautam Adani's family first at $112.7 billion and his second at $86.3 billion.

Why does a record IPO not make him richer overnight? Reliance already owned Jio, and that value was already inside Reliance's share price. The Indian Express worked out a notional promoter holding of about $121 billion if you add Jio separately, and an analyst warned that this counts the same asset twice. __Headlines add, and accountants subtract.__
What he says he wants

In 2027, Reliance celebrates its golden jubilee. He told McKinsey he wants it serving India “even after completing 100 years”. In 2026, he told shareholders that Reliance's “best chapters lie ahead” and laid out the claim for the next decade: AI for all, in 22 languages, and energy India no longer has to import.
The world built its old energy on Middle Eastern oil. The world will now build its new energy on Indian sunshine.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani, 49th AGM, June 2026

blocks.text: Three loose ends remain. The gas disputes are unresolved. The children have not yet been tested without him above them. And both AI and new energy are huge bets whose returns no one can yet see. He said at 59 that “as usual” he would prove the financial community wrong. At 69, he is making the same promise again, this time with his children holding the microphone.

lessons.title: Aim at a billion people, not a billion dollars.
lessons.text: Dhirubhai told his son that starting a business to become a billionaire makes you an idiot. Jio's plan was to bring affordable data to all of India, and the fortune followed. Pick a problem that is big enough to pull talent and customers toward you.

lessons.title: Price the worst day before you bet.
lessons.text: Before Jio, Mukesh Ambani told his board the worst case: little return on their own money and a digitised India anyway. He was ready for that outcome before he spent a rupee. Never bet more than you can survive losing.

lessons.title: Write the knowledge down.
lessons.text: In the 1980s polyester business, experts carried plant secrets home in private notebooks, and he replaced them with open procedures. When tragedy hit Reliance's leadership in 1985–86, there was no panic because the plan did not live in one head. If your startup dies when one person quits, fix that first.

lessons.title: Put young people beside the best in the world.
lessons.text: Short of money, Reliance still paid DuPont $5 million and sat 25-year-olds next to its experts. It bought skill and spread it. Spend on learning from the best before you spend on anything that looks impressive.

lessons.title: Hire character. Train competence.
lessons.text: He told McKinsey character matters more than competence, because competence can be built. Decades of old friends like Manoj Modi and Anand Jain show what trust is worth at scale. Skills you can teach, and honesty you cannot.

lessons.title: Finish one bath before you start another.
lessons.text: He signed a Microsoft joint venture in the 1990s and walked away because there was “too much soap” still on him from chemicals. Reasonable people may say he missed a boom. Even so, turning down a good thing to finish the main thing is what most founders never manage.

lessons.title: Let the young overrule you.
lessons.text: A Yale student's complaint and a son's “Dad, you won’t get it” helped push him into Jio at a time when his own world ran on oil and voice calls. He says he is happy to be overruled. Find someone who can tell you that you are out of date, then actually listen.

lessons.title: Set a price that sounds impossible.
lessons.text: His rule was to build whatever America builds in dollars as if a dollar were worth Rs 10. It forces new design instead of small savings. Set the cost target first, and let it make you rethink everything.

lessons.title: Find your Manoj Modi.
lessons.text: Ambani's college classmate has spent decades turning his ideas into contracts, networks and stores. A visionary without an executor is just a talker. Look for the friend who enjoys the hard, boring work you avoid, and treat them like gold.

lessons.title: Put it on paper while you still like each other.
lessons.text: Dhirubhai left no will, and his sons fought for years, in public and in court. The war cost Mukesh his telecom business until 2010. Write down your shareholding and exit rules on the day your co-founder is still your best friend.

lessons.title: Do not celebrate a deal before it closes.
lessons.text: The $15 billion Aramco sale was announced in 2019, was non-binding, and was gone by 2021, while the Rs 24,713 crore Future deal died at the hands of creditors. He could survive both because Jio raised money elsewhere. You almost certainly could not, so keep a second path ready.

lessons.title: Promise only what you can actually deliver.
lessons.text: Reliance's KG-D6 plan promised 80 million cubic metres of gas a day, and output collapsed to under 10 within years. The promise is still costing lawyers and headlines, with a government claim above $30 billion being contested. Your forecast becomes your reputation the moment someone else relies on it.

lessons.title: Be careful buying into someone else's boom.
lessons.text: He praised the patient leopard in 2011, yet a year earlier he had rushed into American shale while the industry was bullish. A stake bought for $392 million later sold for $126 million. When everyone is shopping in the same aisle, slow down.

lessons.title: Respect the small rules.
lessons.text: Reliance's 2007 trades through 12 agents led to 19 years of cases, and the Supreme Court finally threw out the fraud finding in 2026. Yet the penalty for breaking disclosure rules stayed. A shortcut that saves a little today can follow you for two decades.

lessons.title: When family needs you, show up.
lessons.text: After 15 years of rivalry, he helped with Anil's Ericsson dues in 2019, a day before the deadline that could have sent his brother to jail. One report says it was an outright payment and not a loan. Businesses can be rebuilt, and many relationships cannot, so know which fight to end.

factCheck.method: Built from primary and first-hand material where possible: Mukesh Ambani's own interviews (Rediff/MoneyLIFE 2007, Pritish Nandy 1998, Economic Times 2011 and 2016, McKinsey 2025, ThePrint's Off The Cuff 2016), Reliance documents (the 2018 FT speech, the 2026 AGM Chairman's Statement and event page), Supreme Court orders (2026 INSC 585; Vantara order of 15 Sep 2025), the Competition Commission order of June 2017, plus Reuters, BBC, Bloomberg (via syndication on Al Jazeera, Business Standard), Mint, Economic Times, The Hindu, Indian Express, Business Standard, Forbes and Bloomberg wealth pages. Pages were read through Exa search and fetch. The Off The Cuff quotes come from the YouTube transcript of ThePrint's official video, which is auto-generated, so wording should be spot-checked against the video. The Ken piece is paywalled, and only its free opening was read. Some Economic Times, Mint and Bloomberg items were read as search extracts. Net worth was checked on 1-2 Nov 2026. We found no verified personal social media account; this is a negative finding from our search and from the sibling profile pass, not a statement by Reliance. No former employee was found speaking by name about how he hires or fires; the chapter says so openly. No photo blocks are included in this part because the profile fragment holds the verified Commons photos.

disputed.claim: When Isha told him the home internet 'sucks'
disputed.note: Ambani said 2010 in the 2016 Shekhar Gupta conversation (ET, ThePrint) and 2011 in his March 2018 FT speech. The text gives both.

Times of India 2009 says he rose at 10:30 am and worked noon to midnight; Open 2020 says he works late and starts before noon; Nita Ambani (2013) says he gets home very late. A 2024 Times of India lifestyle piece says 5:30 am yoga but cites only 'various reports'. No first-hand diary exists, so we state the conflict and do not choose.

disputed.claim: Mukesh Ambani's role in the 2019 Ericsson payment
disputed.note: Anil Ambani's statement thanked him for 'timely support'. ET Telecom's sources said about Rs 480 crore, an outright payment and not a loan. Reuters said the nature of the backing was unclear. BBC and Bloomberg said he paid or helped pay. Amount owed is reported as Rs 550 crore plus interest; about Rs 580 crore in total with Rs 118 crore paid earlier; PTI's headline says Rs 462 crore and RCom paid Rs 458.77 crore on the day.

The Guardian said upwards of $600 million; BBC cited planners at $132–156 million and NPR used that range; Al Jazeera called the numbers thinly sourced and speculative. The family has not disclosed a figure, so none is stated as fact in the text.

Press reports put it at $1 billion or more (Crabtree calls $1 billion 'rumoured'; lower-quality sites go up to $4.6 billion). Bloomberg's wealth index lists 'Mumbai Residential Property' at $410 million. We give the $1 billion-plus press range and the Bloomberg figure.

The Times of London quoted him in May 2011. Tata Sons said the report was out of context and factually incorrect, and that the remarks were about wider disparity; The Times stood by its story (Rediff). The text presents both.
Reports based on Nita Ambani (2024) call him strictly vegetarian. In an older Upper Crust interview he said he had always been vegetarian but ate eggs. Text reflects both.

disputed.claim: Jio IPO size and first-day value
disputed.note: Reuters and Forbes say about $3.2 billion; Bloomberg and NYT say $3.1 billion; Times of India gives Rs 30,213 crore. Market value varies by time of day: about $131.5–137 billion. Opening price is given as Rs 1,358 or Rs 1,359; Reuters gives the Rs 1,417.5 close, which we use.

Forbes real-time: $80.3B, #25 (1 Nov 2026). Bloomberg: $77.3B, #24 (31 Oct 2026). Reuters called him Asia's richest according to Forbes on 28 Oct; VnExpress, citing Forbes on 29 Oct, called him Asia's second-richest behind Zhang Yiming; Bloomberg called him Asia's third-richest on 28 Oct. Forbes India's list (family wealth, prices of 11 Sep) has him at $86.3B behind the Adani family at $112.7B; we read this through a Billionaires.Africa summary, not the Forbes page itself.

disputed.claim: Supreme Court result in the Reliance Petroleum case (29 May 2026)
disputed.note: Reuters and The Hindu stress relief for Reliance: fraud finding and Rs 447 crore order set aside, Rs 250 crore refunded. The Economic Times adds that the Rs 25 crore SEBI penalty stands; The Hindu says the Court agreed with the penalty for breaching disclosure rules. We have not read all 135 pages of the judgment and rely on these reports for the operative result.

disputed.claim: Size of KG-D6 government claim and arbitration status
disputed.note: Outlook India's December 2025 report of a claim above $30 billion rests on unnamed sources; Reliance and BP did not comment. It said an award was expected in 2026, and we found no report of one by 2 Nov 2026. This is separate from the $2.81 billion gas-migration dispute now before a Supreme Court-appointed mediator.

The Supreme Court (15 Sep 2025) accepted its SIT's finding of no violation and closed the complaints. The CITES Secretariat's later report (as reported by Mongabay) found no imports without permits but raised concerns about India's due diligence and recommended pausing some imports. Both stated.

disputed.claim: When he left Stanford and the family succession structure
disputed.note: This part avoids dating his Stanford exit (see part-1). The Walton-style trust and family council are reports based on unnamed people (Bloomberg, Mint), never confirmed by Reliance, and are worded that way.
